questions.question: What does the chapter opener call 'the fundamental issue in machine learning'?
questions.answer: The tension between generalization and optimization.
questions.explanation: It is the first bullet of the 'This chapter covers' box.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT listed in 'This chapter covers'?
options: Evaluation methods for machine learning models
Best practices to improve model fitting
Best practices to achieve better generalization
Training convnets on image data
questions.answer: Training convnets on image data
questions.explanation: The first three are bullets in the box. Convnets come later in the book (chapter 8).

questions.question: According to the intro paragraph, what 'central problem of machine learning' did you witness in chapter 4?
questions.answer: Overfitting.
questions.explanation: This is stated directly in the introductory paragraph.

questions.question: Why would accurate model evaluation be emphasized in a chapter about generalization?
questions.answer: Generalization cannot be observed on training data. It can only be estimated on held-out data, so every decision about fit and regularization depends on a trustworthy evaluation.
questions.explanation: This is an interpretation of the intro paragraph, consistent with the training/validation/test split recalled at the start of 5.1.

questions.question: For each chapter 4 example, can you recall how many epochs were chosen and what evidence of overfitting led to that choice?
questions.answer: IMDb: 4 epochs (validation peaked at epoch 4). Housing: 130 epochs (validation MAE stopped improving after 120-140). Reuters: 9 epochs (the model begins to overfit after nine epochs, p.147).
questions.explanation: Revisit p.138, p.147 and p.157 if unsure.

questions.question: Define optimization and generalization as the book does.
questions.answer: Optimization: adjusting a model to get the best performance possible on the training data. Generalization: how well the trained model performs on data it has never seen before.
questions.explanation: These are the definitions in the second paragraph of the page.

questions.question: In figure 5.1, what characterizes the overfitting region?
options: Both training and validation loss decrease
Training loss keeps decreasing while validation loss increases
Both training and validation loss increase
Validation loss is below training loss
questions.answer: Training loss keeps decreasing while validation loss increases
questions.explanation: Overfitting is when generalization degrades while optimization still succeeds. The first option describes underfitting. Training loss does not rise in the figure. Validation loss is never below training loss in figure 5.1.

questions.question: Why does the book say 'you don't control generalization'?
questions.answer: Training only minimizes loss on the training data. Performance on unseen data is a consequence of that fitting, influenced indirectly, never optimized directly. Fitting too well leads to overfitting.
questions.explanation: The learning algorithm never sees the unseen data, so it cannot optimize for it.

questions.question: According to the page, a model is underfit when:
options: Its validation loss is rising
There is still progress to be made because it hasn't modeled all relevant patterns in the training data
It has too many parameters
Its test loss is lower than its training loss
questions.answer: There is still progress to be made because it hasn't modeled all relevant patterns in the training data
questions.explanation: This is the book's definition. A rising validation loss indicates overfitting. Parameter count is not the definition. Test below training loss is not what underfitting means.

questions.question: Map figure 4.11 (housing, p.157) onto the regions of figure 5.1. Where are underfitting, robust fit and overfitting?
questions.answer: Underfitting: the steep drop from epoch 10 to about 40-50. Robust fit: around 120-140 epochs according to the book. Overfitting: beyond that, where improvement has stopped and the curve no longer trends down.
questions.explanation: Real curves are noisy and the rise can be subtle, unlike the idealized figure 5.1.

questions.question: Why is the peak-then-degrade validation pattern called 'universal'?
questions.answer: The book says you will see it with any model type and any dataset. All chapter 4 models showed it.
questions.explanation: Any model that keeps fitting its training data eventually learns training-specific patterns.

questions.question: Sketch figure 5.1 from memory and label the training curve, validation curve, underfitting, robust fit and overfitting.
questions.answer: A monotonically decreasing training curve. A validation curve that follows it, reaches a minimum (robust fit), then rises (overfitting). The region left of the minimum is underfitting.
questions.explanation: Compare with the figure on the page.

questions.question: Name the three data conditions under which, according to the book, overfitting is particularly likely.
questions.answer: When the data is noisy, when it involves uncertainty (ambiguity), and when it includes rare features.
questions.explanation: Stated in the second paragraph of the page; each condition becomes its own subsection (noisy training data p.162, ambiguous features p.163, rare features p.164).

questions.question: Why does the book consider mislabeled valid inputs 'even worse' than invalid inputs?
options: They are more numerous in MNIST
They look like normal members of one class but carry another class's label, so fitting them corrupts predictions on similar real inputs
They cannot be loaded by Keras
They make training loss increase
questions.answer: They look like normal members of one class but carry another class's label, so fitting them corrupts predictions on similar real inputs
questions.explanation: The page's example: a 4 close to the mislabeled 4 may be classified as a 9. The book makes no claim about relative frequency; loading is irrelevant; and fitting them actually decreases training loss.

questions.question: A model reaches 100% training accuracy on a dataset with 2% wrong labels. What does that tell you about the model, and what would you expect on the validation set?
questions.answer: It has memorized the wrong labels as well as the correct ones, so it has fit noise. Validation accuracy will be lower than training accuracy, and inputs resembling mislabeled samples are at risk of being misclassified.
questions.explanation: A model can only be 100% right on wrong labels by reproducing them. Following the page's reasoning, this is 'going out of its way to incorporate outliers', which degrades generalization.

questions.question: In figure 5.3, which label is attached to the image that clearly shows a 4?
questions.explanation: The first image of figure 5.3 is a 4 labeled 9 (index 14582); the text uses it as the example. '7' is the label on the image of a 1, '4' is on the image of a 7, and '5' is on the image of a 3.

questions.question: Give an example of an 'invalid input' for MNIST mentioned in the text.
questions.answer: An all-black image (or the unidentifiable shapes in figure 5.2).
questions.explanation: The book says 'Perhaps a MNIST digit could be an all-black image, for instance—or something like figure 5.2.'

questions.question: Can you explain, without looking, why getting a mislabeled training sample 'right' can make a model worse?
questions.answer: Because the model's function is smooth, outputting the wrong class for that sample also shifts predictions for similar inputs towards the wrong class, so real test samples near it get misclassified.
questions.explanation: This is the mechanism behind the page's final sentence and figure 5.4's right panel (p.163).

questions.question: In figure 5.4, what distinguishes the overfit boundary (right) from the robust one (left)?
options: It is a straight line
It loops around individual outlier points to classify them correctly
It ignores the dark class entirely
It is drawn only through the uncertainty zone
questions.answer: It loops around individual outlier points to classify them correctly
questions.explanation: The red dashed boundary contorts to enclose outliers; the green robust boundary is a smooth curve that misclassifies them. Neither is perfectly straight, neither ignores a class, and the uncertainty zone belongs to figure 5.5.

questions.question: Give the two examples the book uses for noise that comes from ambiguity or randomness rather than inaccuracy.
questions.answer: Classifying banana images as unripened/ripe/rotten (no objective boundaries between categories), and predicting rain from atmospheric pressure (same measurements, different outcomes with some probability).
questions.explanation: Both are in the 'Ambiguous features' paragraph; the first is about subjective categories, the second about inherent randomness.

questions.question: Why can't cleaning the labels remove the noise in the rain-prediction example?
questions.answer: Because the labels are not wrong: identical pressure readings really are followed sometimes by rain and sometimes by clear sky. The uncertainty is in the phenomenon, not in the annotation.
questions.explanation: The book contrasts this with p.162's inaccuracy noise; here even 'perfectly clean and neatly labeled data' is noisy.

questions.question: According to the page, how does a model overfit probabilistic data?
options: By being too confident about ambiguous regions of the feature space
By using too small a learning rate
By predicting 50/50 everywhere
By ignoring the training data
questions.answer: By being too confident about ambiguous regions of the feature space
questions.explanation: That is the page's last paragraph. Learning rate is unrelated here; predicting 50/50 everywhere would be underfitting; ignoring training data is not overfitting.

questions.question: For an input where the true chance of rain is 0.7, compute the expected binary cross-entropy (natural log) of a model predicting 0.7 and of one predicting 0.99.
questions.answer: About 0.611 for the 0.7 prediction, and about 1.389 for the 0.99 prediction.
questions.explanation: Expected loss is −[0.7 ln p + 0.3 ln(1−p)]. For p=0.7: −(0.7·(−0.357)+0.3·(−1.204)) ≈ 0.611. For p=0.99: −(0.7·(−0.010)+0.3·(−4.605)) ≈ 0.007+1.382 ≈ 1.389. Overconfidence more than doubles the expected loss (this calculation is not in the book).

questions.question: Can you sketch figure 5.5 from memory and point out the 'Area of uncertainty' and the two boundaries?
questions.answer: Light and dark point clouds overlapping in a shaded central band; on the left a green dashed line runs simply through the band; on the right a red dashed curve winds in loops around individual points inside the band.
questions.explanation: Being able to reproduce the figure shows you understand the geometric meaning of overfitting in an ambiguous region.

questions.question: Why does a poorly regularized sentiment model classify cherimoya texts as negative?
options: Cherimoya is a negative word in English
The only training text containing it was negative, so the model gave the word a large negative weight
The word is out of vocabulary
Sentiment models ignore rare words
questions.answer: The only training text containing it was negative, so the model gave the word a large negative weight
questions.explanation: The page explains it as a rare-feature spurious correlation. The book notes there is 'nothing negative about the cherimoya'; out-of-vocabulary words would be ignored, not weighted; and the problem is precisely that the model doesn't ignore rare words.

questions.question: What are the shapes of train_images_with_noise_channels and train_images_with_zeros_channels?
questions.explanation: train_images is reshaped to (60000, 784); concatenating a (60000, 784) block along axis=1 doubles the feature dimension.

questions.question: Both added blocks carry zero information about the digit. Why might the noise block hurt validation accuracy while the zero block doesn't?
questions.answer: Zero columns are constant, contribute nothing to the Dense layer's output and get zero gradient. Noise columns vary per sample, so the model can fit chance correlations between noise patterns and labels, and those correlations don't hold on new data.
questions.explanation: This is the spurious-correlation mechanism the page describes; the result is shown on p.166.

questions.question: A neutral word appears in n = 100 training reviews. What is the standard error of the observed positive fraction, and how many standard errors from 50% is the book's 54%?
questions.explanation: This (AI-added) calculation shows that the 54/46 split is well within chance variation, which is why the book calls it a possible 'statistical fluke'.

questions.question: In Listing 5.1, what does axis=1 in np.concatenate do?
options: Adds 784 new samples
Adds 784 new feature columns to each sample
Flattens the images
Normalizes pixel values
questions.answer: Adds 784 new feature columns to each sample
questions.explanation: axis=1 is the feature axis of a (samples, features) matrix. Adding samples would be axis=0; flattening is done by reshape; normalization by / 255.

questions.question: What lesson does the orange-tabby anecdote teach, and how is it corrected?
questions.answer: Generalizing from two cats that share a color and a temperament is overfitting to a tiny sample; meeting a wider variety of cats would show color doesn't correlate with character.
questions.explanation: The book's own conclusion: exposure to more varied data reveals the correlation to be spurious.

questions.question: Could you write Listing 5.1 from memory, including the correct shapes and axis?
questions.answer: Load MNIST, reshape to (60000, 784), cast to float32 and divide by 255, then np.concatenate([x, np.random.random((len(x), 784))], axis=1) and the same with np.zeros.
questions.explanation: Recreating it checks your grasp of the reshape/concatenate mechanics.

questions.question: Why does Listing 5.2 call get_model() a second time before training on the zeros dataset?
options: To change the optimizer
To start from a fresh, untrained model so both runs are comparable
Because Keras models can only be fit once
To load pretrained weights
questions.answer: To start from a fresh, untrained model so both runs are comparable
questions.explanation: Reusing the first model would continue from weights trained on noise data. The optimizer is the same (adam); Keras models can be fit repeatedly; no pretrained weights are involved.

questions.question: With validation_split=0.2 on 60,000 samples, how many samples are used for training and how many for validation?
questions.answer: 48,000 for training and 12,000 for validation.
questions.explanation: 20% of 60,000 is 12,000, taken from the end of the arrays.

questions.question: How many trainable parameters does the first Dense layer have when the input has 1,568 features? How does that compare with plain 784-feature MNIST?
questions.explanation: A Dense layer has (inputs × units) weights plus one bias per unit. Doubling the inputs roughly doubles the count.

questions.question: What does the format string "b-" in Listing 5.3 specify?
options: Bold line
Blue solid line
Blue dashed line
Bar chart
questions.answer: Blue solid line
questions.explanation: In matplotlib, 'b' is blue and '-' is a solid line. A dashed line would be '--' (used for the zeros curve, "r--", on p.166).

questions.question: Why is sparse_categorical_crossentropy the right loss here rather than categorical_crossentropy?
questions.answer: train_labels are integer class indices (0-9), not one-hot vectors; the sparse variant accepts integer targets directly with a 10-way softmax output.
questions.explanation: categorical_crossentropy would require one-hot encoded labels of shape (60000, 10).

questions.question: Can you list the keys you'd expect in history_noise.history and say which one Listing 5.3 plots?
questions.answer: 'loss', 'accuracy', 'val_loss', 'val_accuracy'; Listing 5.3 plots 'val_accuracy'.
questions.explanation: Keras logs the loss plus each compiled metric, for training and (because of validation_split) for validation.

questions.question: According to figure 5.6 and the text, how much lower does the noise-channel model's validation accuracy end up?
options: About 10 percentage points
About 1 percentage point
About 0.01 percentage points
It ends higher
questions.answer: About 1 percentage point
questions.explanation: The text says 'about one percentage point lower'; the plot ends near 0.965 vs. 0.977. The other options contradict the figure.

questions.question: Why does the book say the drop is 'purely' due to spurious correlations?
questions.answer: Because the experiment holds everything else fixed: same model, training settings and information content. The only difference is whether the extra columns vary randomly (and can be fit by chance) or are constant zeros.
questions.explanation: This is the controlled design of Listings 5.1-5.2 (pp.164-165).

questions.question: Describe the typical feature selection procedure the book outlines.
questions.answer: Compute a usefulness score for each feature, a measure of how informative it is for the task such as its mutual information with the labels, and keep only the features whose score exceeds a threshold.
questions.explanation: Stated in the last paragraph; the book notes this would remove the white-noise channels.

questions.question: Which earlier preprocessing step does the book call 'a crude form of feature selection'?
options: Dividing MNIST pixels by 255
Restricting IMDB data to the top 10,000 most common words
One-hot encoding Reuters labels
Using validation_split=0.2
questions.answer: Restricting IMDB data to the top 10,000 most common words
questions.explanation: Quoted directly. Scaling and one-hot encoding transform features without removing any; validation_split selects samples, not features.

questions.question: A binary label has entropy H(Y) = 1 bit. Feature A leaves H(Y|A) = 1 bit; feature B leaves H(Y|B) = 0.4 bits. Compute the mutual information of each with the label. Which would a threshold of 0.1 bits keep?
questions.answer: I(A;Y) = 0 bits, I(B;Y) = 0.6 bits; only B is kept.
questions.explanation: I(X;Y) = H(Y) − H(Y|X). Feature A behaves like a white-noise channel (formula added beyond the book).

questions.question: In Listing 5.3, what do "r--" and plt.xticks(epochs) do?
questions.answer: "r--" draws the zeros curve as a red dashed line; plt.xticks(epochs) puts x-axis ticks at each integer epoch 1-10.
questions.explanation: Standard matplotlib format string and tick control, matching figure 5.6's appearance.

questions.question: Can you predict what figure 5.6 would look like with 3 × 784 noise channels instead of 784, and justify it?
questions.answer: The noise curve would sit even lower, with a larger gap to the zeros curve, because there are more varying meaningless features to find chance correlations in.
questions.explanation: The book states 'The more noise channels you might add, the further accuracy would degrade.'

questions.question: What happens when the model in Listing 5.4 is trained on shuffled MNIST labels?
options: Training loss stays flat and validation loss falls
Training loss goes down while validation loss does not improve
Both losses go down together
Training fails with an error
questions.answer: Training loss goes down while validation loss does not improve
questions.explanation: As stated on the page: the model memorizes training labels but can't generalize. The first option reverses the behaviour; the third would require a real input-label relationship; nothing in the code errors.

questions.question: What validation accuracy would you expect from Listing 5.4, and why?
questions.answer: About 10%: validation labels are random among 10 classes, so no learned rule can beat chance.
questions.explanation: The book says there is 'no possibility of generalization in this setting'; chance level for 10 balanced classes is 1/10.

questions.question: Why does the book compare a memorizing model to a Python dictionary?
questions.answer: A dict stores exact key → value pairs and has no notion of similarity between keys, so it is perfect on stored keys and useless on new ones. A memorizing model likewise reproduces training targets without any rule that transfers.
questions.explanation: It makes concrete the difference between storing samples and learning structure.

questions.question: According to the book, where does generalization in deep learning mainly come from?
options: The specific optimizer used
The number of epochs
The structure of information in the real world
Using softmax outputs
questions.answer: The structure of information in the real world
questions.explanation: Quoted directly. The optimizer, epoch count and output activation are the same or irrelevant across the memorization and generalization cases.

questions.question: In Listing 5.4, does np.random.shuffle(random_train_labels) leave train_labels unchanged? Explain.
questions.answer: No. For a NumPy array, train_labels[:] is a view sharing the same memory, so shuffling it in place also shuffles train_labels. The callout's 'Copies' is only true for Python lists; use .copy() for a real copy.
questions.explanation: np.shares_memory(train_labels[:], train_labels) returns True. In this listing it doesn't change the result, because the unshuffled labels aren't used afterwards.

questions.question: How many trainable parameters does the Listing 5.4 model have, and how does that compare with the number of training samples?
questions.answer: 784·512 + 512 = 401,920 plus 512·10 + 10 = 5,130, for 407,050 total, versus 48,000 training samples (after validation_split=0.2).
questions.explanation: Many more parameters than samples gives ample capacity to memorize each label, consistent with the page's claim that a model with enough parameters can fit anything.

questions.question: Can you explain in two sentences why 'my model reached low training loss' is not evidence that it learned the task?
questions.answer: Because a model with enough capacity reaches low training loss even on random labels, purely by memorizing. Only held-out performance shows whether it captured transferable structure.
questions.explanation: This is the main lesson of Listing 5.4.

questions.question: How many distinct raw MNIST inputs are possible? Express the answer as a power of 2 and as an approximate power of 10.
questions.explanation: There are 28 × 28 = 784 pixels, each with 256 possible uint8 values, giving 256^784. Since 256 = 2^8, this is 2^(8·784) = 2^6272, and 6272 × log10(2) ≈ 1888, so about 10^1888.

questions.question: Which two properties of the subspace of valid handwritten digits does the page emphasize?
options: It is continuous and connected
It is linear and finite
It is uniformly random and dense
It is discrete and disconnected
questions.answer: It is continuous and connected
questions.explanation: The page says the subspace is continuous (small modifications keep the digit recognizable) and connected (smooth paths link any two digits). It is not linear (it is a curved manifold), not uniformly random (it is 'highly structured'), and certainly not disconnected.

questions.question: Why is a smooth curve in the plane a 1D manifold, according to the book?
questions.answer: Because at every point of the curve you can draw a tangent — the curve is approximated by a line at every point, so it is locally like 1D Euclidean space.
questions.explanation: The book defines a manifold as a lower-dimensional subspace locally similar to a Euclidean space; the tangent line is the local 1D Euclidean approximation.

questions.question: Figure 5.7 shows a 3 morphing into a 6. What does the existence of such a sequence tell us, and what would it mean if no such sequence existed?
questions.answer: It shows the digit subspace is connected by smooth paths where consecutive images are very close and all look digit-like. If no such path existed, the region of valid digits would be fragmented, and nearness between samples would carry less information for understanding new samples.
questions.explanation: Connectedness plus continuity is what allows interpolation (p.169): you can relate an unseen point to nearby known points along the manifold.

questions.question: What does the manifold hypothesis claim?
options: Natural data lies on a low-dimensional manifold within its high-dimensional encoding space
Neural networks are manifolds of dimension equal to their parameter count
Any dataset can be compressed losslessly to two dimensions
Data must be preprocessed onto a manifold before training
questions.answer: Natural data lies on a low-dimensional manifold within its high-dimensional encoding space
questions.explanation: This is the book's statement. The second option confuses data with the model; the third overstates — the manifold is low-dimensional but not necessarily 2D, and nothing is said about lossless compression; the fourth is wrong because the structure is a property of the raw data itself.

questions.question: How does this page help resolve the puzzle from p.167 that models can fit randomly shuffled labels?
questions.answer: Fitting ability alone does not explain generalization. Generalization comes from the structure of real data: inputs lie on a continuous, connected low-dimensional manifold, so a model fitted to samples on it can make sense of new nearby points. Random labels destroy any such structure in the input–label relationship, so only memorization is possible.
questions.explanation: p.167 says the explanation has 'rather little to do with deep learning models themselves and much to do with the structure of information in the real world'; this page describes that structure.

questions.question: Can you explain, without using the word 'manifold', why 60,000 training digits can be enough to recognize new digits even though there are ~10^1888 possible images?
questions.answer: Self-check: mention that real digits fill only a tiny, organized region of image space, that nearby points in that region are similar digits, and that a sample can describe the region.
questions.explanation: If you can articulate this, you have the core intuition the next pages build on.

questions.question: In figure 5.8, why is the pixel average of a 2 and a 0 not a valid digit?
options: Linear interpolation in the encoding space leaves the curved digit manifold
The average overflows the uint8 range
Only the model's last layer can compute averages
Averages are always valid digits; the figure shows a rendering error
questions.answer: Linear interpolation in the encoding space leaves the curved digit manifold
questions.explanation: The straight segment between two points on a curved manifold generally passes off the manifold, producing an overlay. Overflow is not the issue (the average of values in 0–255 stays in range); model layers are irrelevant to the figure; and the book explicitly says the average usually isn't a digit.

questions.question: List the two implications of the manifold hypothesis given on this page.
questions.answer: (1) Models only have to fit relatively simple, low-dimensional, highly structured subspaces (latent manifolds) of their input space. (2) Within a manifold it is always possible to interpolate between two inputs via a continuous path that stays on the manifold.
questions.explanation: These are the two bullets on the page.

questions.question: Explain how interpolation lets a model 'make sense of the totality of the space using only a sample of the space.'
questions.answer: Unseen inputs lie on the same manifold as training inputs and close to some of them; by relating a new input to its nearby training points along the manifold, the model can infer how to treat it, filling the gaps between samples.
questions.explanation: This works only if the sample covers the manifold densely enough that every new point has close neighbours (p.171).

questions.question: What does the book mean by local generalization?
options: Making sense of inputs very close to what has been seen before, via interpolation
Generalizing only within one GPU's memory
Generalizing to any input within the input space
Using abstraction and logic to handle novel situations
questions.answer: Making sense of inputs very close to what has been seen before, via interpolation
questions.explanation: Local generalization is what interpolation enables. Option 3 overstates its reach; option 4 describes extreme generalization; option 2 is unrelated.

questions.question: Why does the book use the example of spending a week each in NYC, Shanghai and Bangalore?
questions.answer: To illustrate extreme generalization: humans cope with radically new situations without being trained on many examples of each, something interpolation alone cannot achieve.
questions.explanation: Each city is novel; interpolation from past samples wouldn't cover it, yet humans adapt using reason, abstraction and common sense.

questions.question: Two 'images' have pixels A = [0, 255, 255, 0] and B = [255, 255, 0, 0]. Compute the linear interpolation at t = 0.5 and say why such averages tend to look unlike either input.
questions.answer: x(0.5) = [127.5, 255, 127.5, 0]. Pixels where the images disagree become half-bright, so the result is a faint overlay of both shapes rather than a new shape.
questions.explanation: Linear interpolation averages pixel-wise; regions belonging to only one image are dimmed, producing the ghostly look of the bottom image in figure 5.8.

questions.question: Can you name the cognitive mechanisms the book lists as enabling extreme generalization, and say which family deep learning belongs to?
questions.answer: Abstraction, symbolic models of the world, reasoning, logic, common sense, innate priors (reason). Deep learning belongs with intuition and pattern recognition, which are largely interpolative.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph and its continuation on p.170 draw this contrast.

questions.question: Why must a deep learning model implement a smooth, continuous mapping, according to the page?
options: Because it must be differentiable to be trained with gradient descent
Because GPUs can only compute smooth functions
Because the training data is always linear
Because smooth functions use fewer parameters
questions.answer: Because it must be differentiable to be trained with gradient descent
questions.explanation: The book says smoothness and continuity are necessary for differentiability, without which gradient descent is impossible. GPUs compute any arithmetic; data is not linear (it's a curved manifold); smoothness says nothing about parameter count.

questions.question: What does the paper-ball metaphor say a deep learning model does?
questions.answer: It uncrumples paper balls — it disentangles latent manifolds (the sheet of paper being a 2D manifold in 3D space).
questions.explanation: Stated directly in the first paragraph under 'Why deep learning works', recalling chapter 2.

questions.question: A network can memorize random labels (p.167). Using this page's argument, explain why the same network can still generalize on real MNIST data.
questions.answer: Real data lies on a structured low-dimensional manifold, and gradient descent fits the smooth model curve gradually. Before reaching memorization, training passes through a state where the curve roughly follows the data manifold; at that point interpolation on the model's curve approximates interpolation on the true manifold, so new inputs are handled well. Random labels have no such structure, so only memorization is possible.
questions.explanation: Combines the manifold hypothesis with the gradual fitting argument of e08.

questions.question: What happens, per the book, if you let a sufficiently large model train for very long?
options: It effectively memorizes its training data and won't generalize
It converges exactly to the true data manifold
Its curve becomes linear
Its gradients become undefined
questions.answer: It effectively memorizes its training data and won't generalize
questions.explanation: The book says exactly this. It does not converge to the true manifold (that is only roughly achieved at an intermediate point); nothing makes it linear; gradients remain defined.

questions.question: Where do the 'additional constraints on its structure' of the model curve come from, and why might they help?
questions.answer: From model architecture priors. They restrict the curve to shapes that mirror the structure of the data (e.g. image or sequence structure), making it easier to approximate the latent manifold.
questions.explanation: The page mentions architecture priors in parentheses; p.171 elaborates them as the second property suiting deep learning to manifold learning.

questions.question: What practical training technique follows directly from the existence of a well-generalizing intermediate point in training?
questions.answer: Monitoring validation performance and stopping (or keeping the checkpoint) at the epoch where validation performance is best — early stopping.
questions.explanation: Early stopping is covered in section 5.4.3 (p.185); this page provides its rationale (inference linking the two).

questions.question: Can you sketch, on paper, a set of noisy points along a curve and draw (a) an underfit, (b) a good intermediate, and (c) a memorizing model curve — and say which one interpolates well?
questions.answer: Self-check: (b) follows the underlying curve and interpolates well; (a) misses the shape; (c) passes through every point and wiggles wildly between them.
questions.explanation: This mirrors figure 5.10 referenced on this page.

questions.question: In figure 5.10, which state performs best on new data points?
options: The intermediate robust fit
The final state with perfect training loss
The random initial state
All states perform equally on new data
questions.answer: The intermediate robust fit
questions.explanation: The test-time panels show the robustly fit model handling new points well and the overfit model misclassifying them. The random state is worse still, and the states clearly differ.

questions.question: What is the second property, given on this page, that makes deep learning models well suited to learning latent manifolds?
questions.answer: They are structured to mirror the 'shape' of information in their training data via architecture priors (e.g. image and sequence models), and they build hierarchical, modular representations echoing the organization of natural data.
questions.explanation: The first property (smooth, continuous mapping) was on p.170; this bullet is the second.

questions.question: The book says generalization is more a consequence of the data than of the model. Give two pieces of evidence from pp.167–171 supporting this.
questions.answer: (1) The same model that generalizes on MNIST can only memorize when labels are shuffled (p.167) — the difference is the data's structure. (2) Generalization requires the data to form an interpolable manifold and to be densely sampled; better, less noisy features improve generalization (p.171).
questions.explanation: Both point to the data's structure, not model capacity, as the decisive factor.

questions.question: Where is dense sampling especially important, according to the page?
options: Near decision boundaries
Far from any class boundary
In regions of pure noise
Only in the test set
questions.answer: Near decision boundaries
questions.explanation: The book explicitly says this. Regions far from boundaries are easy to interpolate; noise regions are off-manifold; and the requirement concerns the training data.

questions.question: Why does 'deep learning is curve fitting' imply that a dense sampling is required?
questions.answer: A fitted curve is only constrained where there are data points; between distant points its shape is undetermined by evidence, so interpolation there is unreliable. Dense coverage keeps gaps small so interpolation is accurate.
questions.explanation: The page links curve fitting to the need for dense sampling; p.172 adds that models do nothing more than crude interpolation between training samples.

questions.question: Why do less noisy, more informative features improve generalization, according to the page?
questions.answer: Because the input space becomes simpler and better structured, making the manifold easier to learn and interpolate on.
questions.explanation: Direct statement in the 'Training data is paramount' paragraph.

questions.question: Looking at the overfit test-time panel of figure 5.10, can you point out which new points are misclassified and explain why?
questions.answer: Self-check: points that fall inside the pockets the overfit boundary carved around memorized outliers are misclassified, because the boundary follows individual training points instead of the overall class structure.
questions.explanation: Compare with the robust panel, where the smooth boundary classifies those points correctly.

questions.question: According to the book, what is the best way to improve a deep learning model?
options: Train it on more or better data
Add more layers
Train it for more epochs
Use a larger learning rate
questions.answer: Train it on more or better data
questions.explanation: Stated directly. More layers or epochs increase capacity/fit and can worsen overfitting; the learning rate concerns optimization, not generalization per se.

questions.question: What two strategies does the page propose when getting more data isn't possible?
questions.answer: Modulate the quantity of information the model is allowed to store, or add constraints on the smoothness of the model curve — i.e. regularization.
questions.explanation: These are the 'next-best solution' in the second paragraph.

questions.question: Explain, using figure 5.11, why sparse sampling leads to incorrect interpolation.
questions.answer: With few samples, the learned smooth curve connects them by shortcuts that skip the loops of the true latent curve, so intermediate points of the model lie off the real manifold and the model's 'interpolations' are wrong.
questions.explanation: Dense sampling pins down every bend, so the learned curve approximates the latent space.

questions.question: Why does limiting how much a network can memorize push it toward patterns that generalize?
questions.answer: Optimization still tries to reduce loss, but with limited capacity it can only afford a few patterns; the ones reducing loss across the most samples are the prominent, regular ones, which are more likely to reflect the true structure of the data and thus generalize.
questions.explanation: This is the mechanism the book gives for regularization.

questions.question: Which of these does the book say ML models have no access to?
options: Common sense, abstract reasoning and external knowledge about the world
Their training data
Gradients of the loss
The priors encoded in their architecture
questions.answer: Common sense, abstract reasoning and external knowledge about the world
questions.explanation: The page says models lack these. Training data and architecture priors are precisely what they do contain; gradients are what training uses.

questions.question: According to the book, what are the only two things you will find in a deep learning model?
questions.answer: The priors encoded in its architecture and the data it was trained on.
questions.explanation: Direct quote from the end of the first full paragraph.

questions.question: For a project you know, can you name one way to get 'better' (not just more) data and one way to regularize?
questions.answer: Self-check: e.g. fixing mislabelled samples or removing noisy features; e.g. using a smaller model or a smoothness penalty.
questions.explanation: Section 5.4 (pp.183–185) develops both kinds of remedies in detail.

questions.question: Why is a separate validation set needed in addition to a test set?
options: Because tuning hyperparameters on the evaluation data leaks information and overfits it, so the final test data must be kept separate
Because the training set is too small to fit the model
Because Keras requires three arguments to fit()
Because test data must be shuffled differently
questions.answer: Because tuning hyperparameters on the evaluation data leaks information and overfits it, so the final test data must be kept separate
questions.explanation: That is the page's argument. The other options are unrelated to the reason: training set size, API requirements and shuffling don't explain the need for three splits.

questions.question: Give an example of a hyperparameter and explain how it differs from a parameter.
questions.answer: The number of layers or the size of a layer. Hyperparameters are configuration choices tuned using validation feedback; parameters are the network's weights learned by gradient descent on the training data.
questions.explanation: These are the book's examples and definitions.

questions.question: The model is never trained on the validation set. How can it still overfit to it?
questions.answer: Through information leaks: every time you modify the model based on validation performance, information about the validation data shapes the model's configuration. Over many iterations the configuration becomes tailored to that particular validation set, giving artificially good validation scores.
questions.explanation: Tuning is a form of learning — a search in configuration space using validation performance as the signal.

questions.question: According to the page, when does tuning on the validation set leave it still reliable?
options: When done only once, for one parameter
When done for every hyperparameter simultaneously
When the validation set is larger than the training set
Never — any single use makes it unreliable
questions.answer: When done only once, for one parameter
questions.explanation: The book says very few bits leak in that case. Tuning many parameters many times leaks significant information; relative size isn't the criterion; and the book doesn't say a single use ruins it.

questions.question: What property should the test set have relative to production data, and why?
questions.answer: It should be as similar as possible to production data, so that the final test score predicts how the deployed model will perform.
questions.explanation: Stated in the first paragraph of 5.2.1.

questions.question: A colleague evaluates 50 model variants on the test set and reports the best score as the model's expected production accuracy. What's wrong?
questions.answer: Selecting among variants by test performance tunes the model on the test set, leaking test information; the reported best score is optimistically biased and no longer an honest measure of generalization.
questions.explanation: The page: 'If anything about the model has been tuned based on test set performance, then your measure of generalization will be flawed.'

questions.question: Can you list the three evaluation recipes previewed at the end of the page and say when the more advanced ones are useful?
questions.answer: Simple hold-out validation, K-fold validation, iterated K-fold validation with shuffling; the advanced ones help when little data is available.
questions.explanation: They are explained starting on p.174.

questions.question: In Listing 5.5, what data is the final model trained on before computing test_score?
options: Only training_data
Only validation_data
training_data and validation_data concatenated
training_data, validation_data and test_data
questions.answer: training_data and validation_data concatenated
questions.explanation: The listing calls model.fit(np.concatenate([training_data, validation_data]), ...): all non-test data. Training only on training_data is what happens during tuning; using validation alone would waste data; including test_data would leak the test set.

questions.question: What symptom tells you that your hold-out validation set is too small?
questions.answer: Different random shuffles of the data before splitting give very different measures of model performance.
questions.explanation: This is the diagnostic stated on the page: high variance of the score across splits means the validation set is not statistically representative.

questions.question: Why does hold-out validation need a validation set in addition to the test set, even though the model is never trained on the test set?
questions.answer: Because tuning hyperparameters based on test performance leaks information about the test set into the model, making the test score optimistically biased. The validation set absorbs that tuning so the test set stays an unbiased final check.
questions.explanation: The page says 'to prevent information leaks, you shouldn't tune your model based on the test set', referring back to the argument on p.173 that tuning is itself a form of learning.

questions.question: You have 600 non-test samples and use K = 3 fold validation. How many samples does each model train on and validate on, and how many models are trained?
questions.answer: Each fold has 200 samples; each model trains on 400 and validates on 200; 3 models are trained.
questions.explanation: Partitions of equal size N/K = 200; training uses the remaining K - 1 = 2 partitions.

questions.question: Why does Listing 5.5 call get_model() a second time before the final fit?
options: To change the architecture
To start training from scratch rather than continuing from the tuned weights
Because evaluate() deletes the model
To load the test data
questions.answer: To start training from scratch rather than continuing from the tuned weights
questions.explanation: The callout says to 'train your final model from scratch on all non-test data'. The architecture is unchanged (same tuned hyperparameters); evaluate() does not delete models; get_model() has nothing to do with data loading.

questions.question: Listing 5.5 shuffles before splitting. Name a situation where this would be a mistake.
questions.answer: When predicting the future from the past (time series): shuffling creates a temporal leak, so the test data should be strictly later than the training data.
questions.explanation: The callout says shuffling is 'usually' appropriate; p.177 explains the arrow-of-time exception.

questions.question: Without looking, sketch Figure 5.12 and write the eight-step skeleton of Listing 5.5 from memory.
questions.answer: Figure: a long 'Training set' block (train on this) next to a short 'Held-out validation set' block (evaluate on this), both under 'Total available labeled data'. Code: set size, shuffle, slice validation, slice training, get_model+fit, evaluate validation, tune loop, get_model+fit on concatenation, evaluate test.
questions.explanation: Check your sketch against the page; the key details are the separate final retraining and the single test evaluation.

questions.question: How is the final K-fold validation score computed?
questions.answer: As the average of the K validation scores, one per fold.
questions.explanation: Stated on the page and implemented by np.average(validation_scores).

questions.question: In Listing 5.6 with len(data) = 900 and k = 3, which indices form validation_data when fold = 1?
questions.explanation: n = 300; the slice is data[300*1 : 300*2] = indices 300-599. 0-299 is fold 0, 600-899 is fold 2, and 300-899 would be two partitions.

questions.question: Why does Listing 5.6 call get_model() inside the loop rather than once before it?
questions.answer: Each fold must train an untrained model from scratch; reusing the model would carry weights learned on data that is another fold's validation set, contaminating its score.
questions.explanation: The callout reads 'Creates a brand-new instance of the model (untrained)'.

questions.question: What does the page say K-fold validation does NOT exempt you from?
options: Shuffling the data
Using a distinct validation set for model calibration
Averaging the scores
Training K models
questions.answer: Using a distinct validation set for model calibration
questions.explanation: Quoted directly. Shuffling, averaging and training K models are parts of the procedure itself, not things it exempts you from.

questions.question: Three folds give validation MAE scores 2.3, 3.5 and 2.9. What is the K-fold score, and what does the spread suggest?
questions.answer: 2.9. The spread of 1.2 between folds shows high split-dependence, exactly the case where K-fold beats a single hold-out split.

questions.question: What is wrong with `np.concatenate(data[:a], data[b:])` as printed, and how do you fix it?
questions.answer: np.concatenate expects a sequence of arrays as its first argument; the second positional argument is axis. Write np.concatenate([data[:a], data[b:]]).
questions.explanation: Not stated in the book; it is a NumPy API detail. Listing 5.5 uses the correct list form.

questions.question: Redraw Figure 5.13 for K = 4 and write down which partition validates in each fold.
questions.answer: Four rows; in fold i the i-th of four boxes is 'Validation' and the other three 'Training'; four scores feed an average.
questions.explanation: Generalizes the three-fold figure.

questions.question: You run iterated K-fold with K = 5 and P = 3. How many models are trained and evaluated?
questions.explanation: The page states the count is P * K = 3 * 5.

questions.question: A binary dataset has 90% class A. Which validation accuracy must a model beat to be useful?
questions.explanation: Always predicting A gives 0.9. 0.5 would be the balanced-binary baseline, 0.1 is MNIST's, and 1.0 is perfection, not a baseline.

questions.question: Why is the Reuters baseline about 0.18-0.19 rather than 1/46?
questions.answer: Because the 46 classes are imbalanced: a few topics are much more frequent, so random guessing that follows the class distribution is right more often than 1/46.
questions.explanation: The page attributes the figure to class imbalance.

questions.question: What does it tell you when your model cannot beat a common-sense baseline, according to the book?
questions.answer: That the model is worthless as is: either you are using the wrong model, or the problem may not be approachable with machine learning; go back to the drawing board.
questions.explanation: Direct from the last paragraph of section 5.2.2.

questions.question: Which situation is iterated K-fold validation designed for?
options: Huge datasets where training is slow
Relatively little data and a need for very precise evaluation
Time-series forecasting
Datasets with duplicate samples
questions.answer: Relatively little data and a need for very precise evaluation
questions.explanation: Stated in the first sentence. For huge datasets hold-out suffices; time series must not be shuffled (p.177); duplicates are a separate pitfall (p.177).

questions.question: Explain the rocket analogy: what does the altitude meter correspond to, and why does the starting altitude matter?
questions.answer: The altimeter is the validation metric, your only window on an unobservable high-dimensional learning process. The starting altitude is the trivial baseline: without it you cannot tell whether a reading like 15% accuracy means you have taken off.
questions.explanation: From the second and third printed paragraphs of 5.2.2.

questions.question: For a project you know, write down the trivial baseline before thinking about the model. What is it and how would you compute it?
questions.answer: Answers vary: e.g., majority class frequency for classification, training mean for regression, yesterday's value for forecasting.
questions.explanation: The book advises picking the baseline before you start working with the dataset.

questions.question: You are predicting tomorrow's electricity demand from historical data. How should you split?
options: Shuffle, then take 80/20
Use K-fold with shuffling
Put the most recent period in the test set, earlier data in training
Pick test days at random
questions.answer: Put the most recent period in the test set, earlier data in training
questions.explanation: The arrow-of-time rule: test data must be posterior to training data. The other options all mix future data into training, creating a temporal leak.

questions.question: What goes wrong if digit images are sorted by class and you take the first 80% as training data?
questions.answer: The training set contains only classes 0-7 and the test set only classes 8-9, so neither is representative.
questions.explanation: The book's example; the remedy is to shuffle before splitting.

questions.question: Why does the book call testing on part of your training data 'the worst thing you can do', and how does it arise accidentally?
questions.answer: It measures memorization instead of generalization, giving inflated scores that mislead tuning and deployment. It happens when the data contains duplicates and a shuffle-and-split places copies in both sets.
questions.explanation: From the redundancy bullet; the fix is disjoint sets.

questions.question: Training and validation loss both decrease steadily and you beat the baseline, but the validation loss never turns up. Which problem is this?
options: Training doesn't get started
No meaningful generalization
Still underfitting
Temporal leak
questions.answer: Still underfitting
questions.explanation: That is the third problem on the page. Problem 1 would show a flat training loss; problem 2 would fail the baseline; a temporal leak is an evaluation flaw, not a fit pattern.

questions.question: Explain 'To achieve the perfect fit, you must first overfit.'
questions.answer: You don't know in advance how much capacity or training is right; only by going past the point where validation performance peaks can you locate it. Then you regularize or scale back.
questions.explanation: Direct paraphrase of the opening of section 5.3.

questions.question: Why is a stuck training loss 'always something you can overcome'?
questions.answer: Because a model can be fit even to random data (by memorization), so failing to reduce training loss points to a misconfigured gradient descent process rather than an impossible task.
questions.explanation: The sentence beginning 5.3.1; continued on p.178.

questions.question: List the three evaluation pitfalls from section 5.2.3 and one concrete fix for each.
questions.answer: Representativeness: shuffle (or stratify) before splitting. Arrow of time: chronological split. Redundancy: deduplicate so sets are disjoint.
questions.explanation: Check against p.176-177.

questions.question: What is the only difference between the model setups in Listings 5.7 and 5.8?
options: The number of Dense units
The optimizer type
The learning rate
The loss function
questions.answer: The learning rate
questions.explanation: Both use Dense(512, relu) + Dense(10, softmax), RMSprop and sparse categorical crossentropy; only learning_rate changes from 1.0 to 1e-2.

questions.question: Name the four gradient-descent settings the book blames for stalled training.
questions.answer: Choice of optimizer, distribution of initial weight values, learning rate, batch size.
questions.explanation: Listed in the second paragraph of the page.

questions.question: Why is it 'usually sufficient' to tune only learning rate and batch size?
questions.answer: Because the gradient-descent parameters are interdependent: their effects on the size and noise of updates overlap, so adjusting these two covers most fixes while keeping the rest constant.
questions.explanation: The book's reason is interdependence; the explanation of how they overlap is an elaboration.

questions.question: On L(w) = w^2 starting at w = 1, compute two plain gradient-descent steps with learning rate 1.0 and with 0.25. What do you observe?
questions.answer: Gradient is 2w. With 1.0: w goes 1 -> -1 -> 1 (oscillation, no progress). With 0.25: w goes 1 -> 0.5 -> 0.25 (converging).
questions.explanation: Illustrates overshooting from too large a learning rate; an AI-provided toy example, not from the book.

questions.question: In Listing 5.7, what does validation_split=0.2 do?
options: Uses 20% of the test set for validation
Holds out 20% of the training arrays as validation data
Drops 20% of the units
Trains on 20% of the data
questions.answer: Holds out 20% of the training arrays as validation data
questions.explanation: Keras reserves that fraction of train_images/train_labels for validation. The test split was discarded with `_`; dropout is unrelated; training uses the other 80%.

questions.question: Why should training always be possible, even on a meaningless problem?
questions.answer: Because a model can memorize the training data, driving training loss down even without any learnable pattern.
questions.explanation: First sentence of the page, continuing p.177.

questions.question: Run Listing 5.7 yourself, then Listing 5.8, and record the validation accuracy after each epoch. Can you explain the difference?
questions.answer: Expect a plateau at roughly 20-40% for 1.0 and steady improvement to high accuracy for 1e-2.
questions.explanation: Hands-on verification of the page's claim.

questions.question: Training loss decreases but validation accuracy on MNIST stays at 10%. Which explanation does the book give for the shuffled-label experiment?
options: Learning rate too high
Batch size too small
The inputs contain no information about the targets
The model is too small
questions.answer: The inputs contain no information about the targets
questions.explanation: With shuffled labels it is impossible to generalize. Learning rate and batch size issues prevent the training loss itself from falling; a too-small model would still beat 10%.

questions.question: Why might a learning rate that is too low look like the training has stalled?
questions.answer: Each update is so small that the loss decreases extremely slowly, making progress invisible over a few epochs.
questions.explanation: From the first bullet on the page.

questions.question: What are architecture priors, and how does the chapter 13 example illustrate them?
questions.answer: Assumptions about the problem built into a model's structure. On a timeseries task, a densely connected network ignores sequential structure and can't beat a trivial baseline, while a recurrent architecture, whose structure assumes ordered sequences, generalizes well.
questions.explanation: Paraphrase of the fourth printed paragraph of 5.3.2.

questions.question: If increasing the batch size from 64 to 256 is applied, by what factor does the standard deviation of the gradient estimate change (assuming independent samples)?
questions.answer: It halves: variance falls by 4, standard deviation by sqrt(4) = 2.
questions.explanation: Var = sigma^2 / B; this formula is an AI-added formalization of the book's statement that larger batches give lower-variance gradients.

questions.question: Your model fits, validation metrics improve and beat the baseline. According to 5.3.3, what should you do next?
options: Add dropout
Stop and deploy
Get the model to start overfitting
Lower the learning rate
questions.answer: Get the model to start overfitting
questions.explanation: The book: 'Next, you need to get your model to start overfitting.' Dropout comes after overfitting (5.4); deploying is premature; the learning rate is already working.

questions.question: Why does the book call 'trains but doesn't generalize' perhaps the worst ML situation?
questions.answer: Because it signals something fundamentally wrong with the approach (data or modelling assumptions), and unlike a stuck loss, there is no simple knob to turn and it may not be easy to tell what is wrong.
questions.explanation: Second printed paragraph of 5.3.2.

questions.question: For each of the three problems on p.177, state which subsection handles it and one remedy, using p.178-179.
questions.answer: Training doesn't start -> 5.3.1, tune learning rate/batch size. No generalization -> 5.3.2, better data or architecture priors. Can't overfit -> 5.3.3, increase capacity.
questions.explanation: Ties the page back to the roadmap on p.177.

questions.question: What shape of validation-loss curve does the book associate with insufficient model capacity?
options: It decreases, then turns upward
It stalls or improves very slowly without reversing course
It stays flat at the random-guess level from the first epoch
It oscillates wildly from epoch to epoch
questions.answer: It stalls or improves very slowly without reversing course
questions.explanation: Figure 5.14 flattens around 0.26. An upturn is overfitting. A loss stuck at chance level points to an unsolvable problem or a bad architecture prior (p.179). Wild oscillation suggests too high a learning rate.

questions.question: Why is the model in Listing 5.9 a logistic regression?
questions.answer: It is a single Dense layer mapping inputs linearly to 10 scores, followed by softmax: a linear model with softmax probabilities, trained with crossentropy.
questions.explanation: With no hidden layers there is no nonlinearity before the softmax, so it is exactly multinomial logistic regression.

questions.question: How many trainable parameters does Listing 5.9's model have on flattened 28×28 MNIST images?
questions.explanation: The kernel has 784×10 weights and there is one bias per unit.

questions.question: With validation_split=0.2 on the 60,000 MNIST training images, how many images are used for training and how many for validation?
questions.answer: 48,000 for training and 12,000 for validation (the last 20% of the arrays).
questions.explanation: Keras slices off the final fraction of the arrays as validation data before training.

questions.question: Why should you not just train Listing 5.9's model for 200 epochs instead of 20?
questions.answer: The validation loss has already plateaued. The limit is the model's representational power, so more epochs give essentially nothing; you need a bigger model.
questions.explanation: The text notes that you cannot clearly overfit 'even after many iterations' (continued on p.181).

questions.question: Why is 'cannot overfit' a problem rather than a good thing?
questions.answer: A model that cannot overfit lacks the capacity to capture all the useful structure in the data. You want to reach the overfitting regime, then pull back with regularization, so you find the best trade-off.
questions.explanation: The book's position (p.181) is that it should always be possible to overfit, and failing to do so means you need more capacity.

questions.question: Can you sketch, from memory, the three validation curves for a model with too little, appropriate, and too much capacity?
questions.answer: Too little: drops and flattens (Fig. 5.14). Appropriate: drops, reaches a minimum around epoch 8, then rises (Fig. 5.15). Too much: rises almost immediately (Fig. 5.16).
questions.explanation: These three figures form the comparison running through pp.180-182.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the book's ways to increase representational power?
options: Adding more layers
Using bigger layers
Using layer types better suited to the problem
Adding dropout
questions.answer: Adding dropout
questions.explanation: Dropout is a regularization technique that reduces effective capacity (section 5.4). The other three options are the levers listed on this page.

questions.question: Compute the number of trainable parameters in the bigger model (784 → 128 → 128 → 10).
questions.explanation: Each Dense layer has inputs×units weights plus units biases.

questions.question: According to the book, when does the bigger model start overfitting?
questions.answer: After about eight epochs.
questions.explanation: Stated in the text accompanying Figure 5.15.

questions.question: Why does the comparison between Listing 5.9 and the bigger model isolate the effect of capacity?
questions.answer: Optimizer, loss, metrics, epochs, batch size and validation split are identical. Only the architecture changes.
questions.explanation: A controlled experiment attributes the change in curve shape to capacity alone.

questions.question: Figure 5.15's validation loss rises after its minimum. What should you do next, and what should you not do?
questions.answer: Don't increase capacity further. Move on to improving generalization: early stopping at the best epoch, and regularization.
questions.explanation: Overfitting means capacity is sufficient. Section 5.4 covers what to do next.

questions.question: What does the book compare the 'can't overfit' problem to?
options: Data leakage
The training loss doesn't go down
Class imbalance
Exploding gradients
questions.answer: The training loss doesn't go down
questions.explanation: Both are described as issues that can always be solved. Leakage, imbalance and exploding gradients are not mentioned here.

questions.question: Given a new validation curve, can you tell in one look whether to add capacity, regularize, or fix optimization?
questions.answer: Flat at chance → optimization or priors. Improves then plateaus → add capacity. Dips then rises → regularize or stop early. Rises immediately → reduce capacity.
questions.explanation: This sums up the diagnostic logic of section 5.3.

questions.question: How can you tell, per the book, that your model is too large?
options: Its training loss never decreases
It starts overfitting right away
Its validation loss plateaus around a fixed value
It needs more than 20 epochs
questions.answer: It starts overfitting right away
questions.explanation: That is the stated symptom. A training loss that never decreases is an optimization problem (p.178). A plateau means too little capacity (p.180). Epoch count is not a diagnostic.

questions.question: Why does the very-large-model code use batch_size=32 instead of 128?
questions.answer: To limit memory consumption when training a larger model (the printed callout).
questions.explanation: Activation memory grows with batch size times layer width.

questions.question: How many parameters does the 784 → 2048 → 2048 → 2048 → 10 model have?
questions.explanation: Each Dense layer has inputs×units weights plus units biases.

questions.question: With validation_split=0.2 and batch_size=32, how many gradient updates happen per epoch? Compare with batch_size=128.
questions.answer: 48,000/32 = 1,500 updates per epoch, versus 48,000/128 = 375.
questions.explanation: That is four times as many updates per epoch, one reason fitting (and overfitting) happens sooner.

questions.question: When does the book say to switch focus to maximizing generalization?
questions.answer: Once the model has shown some generalization power and is able to overfit.
questions.explanation: That is the opening sentence of section 5.4, consistent with p.177's plan.

questions.question: Comparing Figures 5.15 and 5.16, which model would you deploy if you could stop each at its best epoch, and why?
questions.answer: The 2×128 model. Its best validation loss (about 0.09) is lower than the 3×2,048 model's best (about 0.12, at epoch 1).
questions.explanation: More capacity is not better here: the huge model never goes through a useful learning phase before it starts memorizing.

questions.question: Can you describe the validation-curve signature of each of the three capacity regimes without looking?
questions.answer: Too little: drops and plateaus. Appropriate: dips then rises. Too much: rises from the start.
questions.explanation: Figures 5.14-5.16.

questions.question: Which problem does the book give as an example where deep learning will not help?
options: Image classification
List sorting
Sentiment analysis
Reading a clock
questions.answer: List sorting
questions.explanation: Sorting is fundamentally discrete, with no smooth interpolation. Image and text classification are classic deep learning successes. Clock reading is hard from pixels but solvable.

questions.question: List the four dataset-curation practices on this page.
questions.answer: Have enough data (dense sampling), minimize labeling errors, clean the data and handle missing values, and do feature selection.
questions.explanation: These are the four bullets of section 5.4.1.

questions.question: Why does the book insist on a dense sampling of the input-cross-output space?
questions.answer: Deep learning generalizes by interpolating between training samples on the latent manifold. Gaps in coverage leave regions where interpolation is unreliable.
questions.explanation: This follows from 'generalization originates from the latent structure of your data.'

questions.question: In the book's definition, feature engineering applies which kind of transformations?
options: Learned transformations inside the network
Hardcoded, non-learned transformations before the model
Random augmentations during training
Regularization penalties on the weights
questions.answer: Hardcoded, non-learned transformations before the model
questions.explanation: The definition specifies hardcoded transformations applied before the data reaches the model. Learned layers, augmentation and penalties are different tools.

questions.question: In the clock example, what makes the (x, y) hand-tip features so much better than raw pixels?
questions.answer: They compress thousands of pixels to four directly relevant numbers, so the remaining mapping to time is simple and smooth enough for a simple model, with no convnet or heavy compute.
questions.explanation: Domain knowledge does the hard perception step.

questions.question: Think of a dataset you know. Which curation step would most improve it, and what hardcoded feature could make the model's job easier?
questions.answer: Open-ended.
questions.explanation: Apply the checklist and the definition from this page to your own data.

questions.question: With the 'even better' features in Figure 5.17, what is needed to recover the time?
options: A convolutional neural network
A two-layer MLP
A simple rounding operation and a dictionary lookup
Gradient-boosted trees
questions.answer: A simple rounding operation and a dictionary lookup
questions.explanation: The text says no ML is required once the inputs are angles. The other options are learning methods, which are unnecessary at that point.

questions.question: Using θ = atan2(y, x), verify Figure 5.17's angle for the hand at (x2, y2) = (-0.38, 0.32).
questions.explanation: The point is in the second quadrant, so the angle lies between 90° and 180°.

questions.question: Name three hardcoded features used for MNIST before convnets, according to the book.
questions.answer: Number of loops in a digit image, height of each digit, and a histogram of pixel values.
questions.explanation: These are listed in the 'Before deep learning…' paragraph.

questions.question: Why did feature engineering matter more for shallow algorithms than for deep networks?
questions.answer: Shallow algorithms' hypothesis spaces weren't rich enough to learn useful features themselves, so the representation had to be supplied by hand. Deep networks learn features from raw data.
questions.explanation: See the 'Before deep learning' and 'Fortunately' paragraphs.

questions.question: Give the two reasons the book says feature engineering still matters with deep networks.
questions.answer: (1) Good features solve problems more elegantly with fewer resources. (2) Good features let you solve problems with far less data.
questions.explanation: These are the two bullets at the bottom of the page.

questions.question: Connect feature engineering to the manifold view of generalization.
questions.answer: Feature engineering makes the latent manifold smoother, simpler and better organized. That makes interpolation between samples easier and needs fewer samples to cover the manifold densely.
questions.explanation: This is the book's 'essence' sentence combined with p.183's dense-sampling argument.

questions.question: Can you redo the clock pipeline (pixels → coordinates → angles → time) for a clock showing 6:00?
questions.answer: Minute hand tip about (0, 1) gives θ=90°. Hour hand tip about (0, -0.5) gives θ=270° (or -90°), clock angle 180°, hour 6.
questions.explanation: Apply atan2 and the clock-angle conversion.

questions.question: Why is vast overparameterization not a problem in deep learning, according to the book?
options: Because weight decay is always applied
Because you never fully fit a deep learning model
Because more parameters always generalize better
Because the test set corrects for it
questions.answer: Because you never fully fit a deep learning model
questions.explanation: Training is interrupted long before the minimum training loss. Weight decay isn't mentioned here. More parameters can overfit right away (p.182). The test set is only for final evaluation.

questions.question: What does the Keras EarlyStopping callback do?
questions.answer: It interrupts training as soon as validation metrics stop improving, while remembering the best known model state.
questions.explanation: As stated in section 5.4.3. Details come in chapter 7.

questions.question: What is the drawback of the chapter 4 approach of training long, then retraining for the best epoch count?
questions.answer: It requires redundant work (a second full training run), which can be expensive.
questions.explanation: Saving per-epoch models or EarlyStopping avoids the retraining.

questions.question: Which best describes regularization as defined on this page?
options: Techniques that speed up convergence
Techniques that actively impede a perfect fit to the training data to improve validation performance
Techniques that normalize input features
Techniques that increase model capacity
questions.answer: Techniques that actively impede a perfect fit to the training data to improve validation performance
questions.explanation: This is the book's definition. Faster convergence, input normalization and added capacity are different goals.

questions.question: Why does a smaller network learn more useful representations?
questions.answer: With limited memorization resources it cannot memorize the training data, so to minimize the loss it must learn compressed representations with predictive power about the targets.
questions.explanation: That is the argument of 'Reducing the network's size'.

questions.question: What determines the 'size' of a model in the book's sense?
questions.answer: The number of learnable parameters, determined by the number of layers and the number of units per layer.
questions.explanation: As stated in the parenthetical in 'Reducing the network's size'.

questions.question: Can you explain why 'you will only achieve generalization if you can measure it' connects section 5.2 to section 5.4?
questions.answer: Every regularization choice must be judged on a reliable validation procedure. Without accurate evaluation (section 5.2), you can't tell whether a technique improved generalization.
questions.explanation: Regularizing is an empirical, evaluation-guided process.

questions.question: According to the page, how should you determine the right number of layers and layer sizes?
options: Use a formula based on the number of training samples
Evaluate different architectures on the validation set, starting small and growing until validation loss shows diminishing returns
Evaluate different architectures on the test set and keep the best
Always use the largest model your hardware allows
questions.answer: Evaluate different architectures on the validation set, starting small and growing until validation loss shows diminishing returns
questions.explanation: The book says there is no magical formula (so the first option is wrong) and insists on the validation set, not the test set (so the third is wrong). The largest model overfits badly (p.188), which rules out the fourth.

questions.question: What does validation_split=0.4 do in listing 5.10, and how many reviews end up in validation?
questions.answer: It holds out the last 40% of the training arrays as validation data, evaluated after every epoch. That is 10,000 of the 25,000 reviews, leaving 15,000 for training.
questions.explanation: Keras slices off the final fraction of x and y before training and reports val_loss and val_accuracy for it each epoch.

questions.question: Compute the number of trainable parameters of the reference model (input 10,000, Dense 16, Dense 16, Dense 1).
Why does listing 5.11 keep the optimizer, loss, epochs, batch size and validation split identical to listing 5.10?
questions.answer: To make it a controlled experiment. Only capacity (layer width) changes, so differences in the validation curves can be attributed to model size.
questions.explanation: If several settings changed at once, figure 5.18 could not tell you which one caused the different overfitting behaviour.

questions.question: What does the line results[i, sequence] = 1.0 do inside vectorize_sequences?
questions.answer: It sets to 1.0, in row i, every column whose index appears in the list `sequence`. This is multi-hot encoding through NumPy integer-array indexing.
questions.explanation: `sequence` is a list of word indices, so indexing with it addresses all those positions at once. Repeated indices are simply set to 1 again.

questions.question: Could you explain to a colleague why the test set must not be used to choose model size, and describe the procedure the book recommends instead?
questions.answer: Self-check: choosing on the test set leaks information and biases the final score. Instead, compare sizes on validation data, growing from small until validation loss has diminishing returns.
questions.explanation: See the first paragraph of the page and p.135.

questions.question: What does figure 5.18 show about the smaller (4-unit) model compared with the original?
options: It overfits earlier and more severely
It starts overfitting later (about six epochs rather than four) and degrades more slowly
It never overfits
It has lower validation loss at every epoch
questions.answer: It starts overfitting later (about six epochs rather than four) and degrades more slowly
questions.explanation: This is the book's own reading of the figure. It does overfit eventually (so 'never overfits' is wrong), and in the first epochs its loss is higher (so 'every epoch' is wrong). Earlier and more severe overfitting describes the larger model on p.188.

questions.question: Why is the smaller model's validation loss higher than the original's during the first two or three epochs?
questions.answer: With fewer units it fits the data more slowly. Its limited capacity means each epoch reduces the loss less, so early on it is still underfitting relative to the bigger model.
questions.explanation: Capacity speeds up fitting (p.188: 'the more capacity the model has, the more quickly it can model the training data'). The flip side is a slower start for small models.

questions.question: What is the only difference between listings 5.10 and 5.11?
questions.answer: The hidden layers have 4 units each instead of 16. Data, optimizer, loss, metrics, epochs, batch size and validation split are the same.
questions.explanation: Keeping everything else fixed isolates the effect of capacity.

questions.question: How many parameters does the 4-4-1 model have with 10,000 input features, and by what factor is that smaller than the 16-16-1 model's 160,305?
questions.explanation: 160,305 / 40,029 is about 4.0, because the first layer dominates and its size scales linearly with width.
